beats.text: Several of them showed a real effect. If the study had stopped there, it would have produced a perfectly respectable paper concluding that Everglades amphibians are
declining for the usual complicated mix of reasons.
Then they added one more variable to the model.
Swamp eel presence. Everything else fell away. Once swamp eels were in the model, the other factors stopped explaining much of anything.
Howell's summary of it was that none of the rest matters anymore once you account for the eels, and that it isn't even close.
The eel effect was more than twice the size of any other single factor tested.
That's the finding. Not that swamp eels are one of several stresses, that they are the leading predictor of both how many amphibians a site holds and which
species are in it, across four regions of the largest wetland in the United States.
And there's a geographic signature in the data that makes it even harder to explain any other way.
Because of the nutrient gradient running from north to south, aquatic life in the Everglades was already naturally more abundant in the north than the south.
The eels, spreading up from the southeast, have exaggerated that existing pattern, pushing southern abundance down further,
while the northern strongholds remain loud. Which means the pattern isn't just that amphibians are declining, it's that amphibians are declining in a spatial gradient
that tracks the eel invasion front. And that front is still moving.
The northern Everglades, the part that still gives researchers headaches with the volume of the frog calls, is not a refuge, it's just the part the eels haven't finished reaching.
Twenty years ago, surveys inside Everglades National Park found the southern leopard frog to be one of the most common amphibians in the system.
Ordinary. Everywhere. The kind of animal you don't bother recording carefully, because there will always be more of them.
Howell's team did not detect a single one inside Everglades National Park, from the most common species in the park to functionally absent in about twenty
years. And it happened without a headline, because nobody counts frogs.
The species that are hanging on in the eel-occupied zones are the ones with an escape route.
The tree frogs, up in the canopy. And two large aquatic salamanders, the greater siren and the two-toed amphiuma.
Both are big, both are eel-shaped themselves, both live in the mud.
Which is exactly the problem. They're surviving right now because they're large enough not to be prey.
But they eat the same things the swamp eel eats, in the same places, using the same strategy.
They are not sheltered from the invasion. They are in direct competition with it.
And the researchers expect that competition to start removing them, too.
Then there's the one nobody will notice. The Everglades dwarf siren is a small, eel-like salamander.
A subspecies found in this system, and effectively nowhere else.
Across 30 sites, across an area the size of Delaware, over two months of intensive trapping and surveying, the team did not record one.
Howell's assessment was that it's the kind of animal that could simply blink out of existence, and that almost nothing is known about it.
Think about what that sentence actually contains. There is a species in the United States, in a national park, that may already be gone.
And we would not be able to say when or how many there were before, because nobody ever found out.
Extinctions in the public imagination are large and slow and mournful.
The last of something, filmed, named, grieved over.
This is what most of them actually look like. A subspecies nobody photographed, in water nobody was sampling,
removed by an animal that arrived in a bucket. So what is being done?
Honestly, very little. And not because anyone is being negligent, because the tools don't exist.
Run through the standard invasive species playbook and watch it fail one option at a time.
Physical removal. This is the python model. Pay people to go and catch them.
It works on pythons, because pythons are large, visible when you find them, and worth a bounty.
